This page is the interactive version of the lesson notes (PDF). Each section
starts from a problem in a game, explains the component behind it, and ends
with a **Do it** task (on the lab computer, your phone or the simulator) and
one set of questions. The full explanations, worked examples and exercises

## Key terms

{{< glossary cpu cpu-core clock-rate thread memory-hierarchy cache memory byte texture storage ssd app-storage >}}

## 3.1 Why eight cores do not make a game eight times faster

A **core** is a complete processor that runs one stream of instructions, a
**thread**. A phone CPU usually has a few large **performance cores** and
several small **efficiency cores** that save battery. A game has one **main
thread** that runs the game logic in a fixed order, and **worker threads**
for physics, loading and sound. Only the worker part can be shared among
cores, so more cores help less than you expect: in the notes, a 16 ms frame
(10 ms main thread + 6 ms shared work) takes 11 ms with six cores, not
16/6 ms. The gigahertz value (**clock rate**) describes the pace of one core
only.

![The operating system places each thread on a core.](images/cpu-cores.png){width=94%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
Cores do not add up: 8 cores at 3 GHz are **not** 24 GHz.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch the cores at work"}
On a lab computer: Ctrl + Shift + Esc → Task Manager → **Performance → CPU**.
Right-click the graph → **Change graph to → Logical processors**. Play the
simulator of section 3.2 for 30 seconds and watch. Write down the number of
cores and logical processors, and one sentence on how the work is shared.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Cores and threads"}
A frame needs 8 ms on the main thread and 4 ms of work that can be shared
equally among cores. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="6 ms|a performance core|24 GHz"}
The frame time with one core.
:   12 ms

The frame time with four cores.
:   9 ms

The part of a frame that cannot be shared among cores.
:   the main thread's game logic

The best core for playing music in the background with little battery.
:   an efficiency core

8 cores at 3 GHz: how fast is the main thread's core?
:   3 GHz
:::
:::

## 3.2 Why the processor keeps a small memory beside it

Main memory needs about 100 ns to answer: hundreds of clock ticks of
waiting. So memory is built as a **memory hierarchy**: registers → **cache**
→ main memory → storage. Higher levels are small, fast and close to the
core; lower levels are large, slow and cheap. The cache keeps copies of data
used again and again (the player's position, the code of the game loop). A
**cache hit** is fast (about 1 ns); a **cache miss** goes to main memory
(about 100 ns).

![The memory hierarchy, with typical times.](images/memory-hierarchy.png){width=92%}

{{< sim file="sims/data-trip.html" poster="sims/data-trip.png" title="Data Trip: fetch data through the memory hierarchy" kind="sim" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Fetch the data yourself"}
In **Data Trip**, fetch one value from each level and write the real time and
the human-scale time in a table. Then set the cache hits to 99 %, 90 % and
80 % and write the memory time of the frame each time. End with one sentence:
what does the cache do?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · The memory hierarchy"}
One frame reads memory 1 000 000 times: 1 ns from the cache, 100 ns from main
memory. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="28 hours|50.5 ms|in main memory"}
The player's position is read 50 times in one frame. After the first read, where does the core find it?
:   in the cache

The best score must survive when the phone is switched off. Where is it kept?
:   in storage (flash)

The memory time of the frame with 90 % cache hits.
:   10.9 ms

The memory time of the frame with 99 % cache hits.
:   about 2 ms

If 1 ns lasted 1 second, a read from main memory would last…
:   100 seconds
:::
:::

## 3.3 What a game keeps in memory while you play

Main memory holds what the game needs **now**: code, the assets of the
scene (**textures**, models, sounds) and the game state (positions, health,
score). The operating system and background apps use the same memory.
Textures usually take the largest share. A texture needs
width × height × bytes per pixel: 2048 × 2048 × 4 bytes = 16 MiB, or 4 MiB in
the compressed GPU format ASTC (1 byte per pixel). Storage makers count
**bytes** in powers of 1000 (KB, MB, GB); memory is counted in powers of 1024
(KiB, MiB, GiB).

![Main memory of a phone during play (example values).](images/game-ram.png){width=92%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
A 2 MB PNG file does **not** use 2 MB of memory: it is decoded into raw
pixels before the GPU can draw it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch the memory fill"}
On a lab computer: Task Manager → **Processes**, sort by **Memory**. Write
down the browser's memory. Open five image-heavy pages (gallery, map, video
site), wait ten seconds, and write it down again. What does the extra memory
hold?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Memory sizes"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="2 MB|in powers of 1000|sounds"}
A 1024 × 1024 texture with 4 bytes per pixel.
:   4 MiB

The same texture in ASTC (1 byte per pixel).
:   1 MiB

A 2048 × 2048 texture with 4 bytes per pixel.
:   16 MiB

A game is close to its memory limit. Which assets should the team compress first?
:   textures

A phone shows "3.7 GiB" of RAM. How is this size counted?
:   in powers of 1024
:::
:::

## 3.4 Where the game lives when it is not running

**Storage** keeps the game when the power is off. A **hard disk** uses
spinning magnetic platters and a moving arm (slow, cheap). An **SSD** uses
flash chips with no moving parts; phones have the same flash chips on their
board. In storage, a game has three parts: the **app** (code and built-in
assets), the **user data** (saves, settings, downloaded levels) and the
**cache** (temporary files it can rebuild). A "1 TB" SSD shows as 931 GB in
Windows: the same bytes, counted in powers of 1024.

![Storage technologies and the parts of a game in storage.](images/storage.png){width=94%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
**Clear cache** deletes temporary files. **Clear storage** deletes the
player's data.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A game in your phone's storage"}
**Android:** Settings → Apps → *(a game)* → Storage. **iPhone:** Settings →
General → iPhone Storage → *(a game)*. Write down the size of each part.
Which part would grow if you downloaded a new level? Do **not** press Clear
storage, Offload App or Delete App.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Storage"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="2000 GB|an SSD|Clear cache"}
A laptop loads games slowly, and a moving arm inside it reads the data. Its storage is…
:   a hard disk

The player presses Clear cache on a 300 MB cache. What is lost?
:   nothing important (temporary files)

A player wants to free space but keep the pets. Which button must they avoid?
:   Clear storage

A "2 TB" SSD, as Windows shows it.
:   about 1863 GB

Pocket Pets uses app 1.1 GB, islands 2.4 GB, cache 0.3 GB. What is left after Clear cache?
:   about 3.5 GB
:::
:::

## Game challenge: the Pocket Pets support desk {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

![The Pocket Pets support desk.](images/pocket-pets.png){width=94%}

*Pocket Pets* is a made-up mobile game. Version 2.0 adds an island with 40
textures of 2048 × 2048 pixels, stored in ASTC (1 byte per pixel). The
support desk receives five messages: (1) "My phone has eight cores, but only
one is really busy"; (2) "The island download needs 1.6 GB and my phone has
1.2 GB free"; (3) "I pressed Clear storage and my pets are gone"; (4) "My new
1 TB laptop SSD shows only 931 GB"; (5) "When I enter the island, the pets
look blurry for a second".

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Answer the players (harder)"}
Choose the answer for each message.

::: {.match extra="640 MiB|the cache|1.6 GB"}
Message 1: the work that keeps one core busy.
:   the main thread's game logic

Message 2: how much more free space the player needs.
:   0.4 GB

Message 3: the part of storage that was deleted.
:   the user data

Message 4: why the SSD shows 931 GB.
:   decimal bytes shown in binary units

Message 5: the memory taken by the island's 40 textures.
:   160 MiB
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- A core runs one thread; the main thread stays on one core, so cores do not add up.
- Memory hierarchy: registers → cache → RAM → storage, from fast and small to slow and large.
- The cache keeps data used again and again; hits are about 100 times faster than misses.
- RAM holds code, assets and state; a texture needs width × height × bytes per pixel.
- Storage keeps the app, the user data and the cache; Clear storage deletes the player's data.
